subject: plot occupancy probabilities: very steepy curves

messages.author: 010fa11e67a0d0b7
messages.subject: plot occupancy probabilities: very steepy curves
parts:
Dear all,

I am plotting the predicted occupancy probabilities resulting from different models, and aggainst different variables.
My 'problem' is, that absolutely all my curves, independently of model and variable are very steepy. So, at a given value the occupancy probability increases or decreases very fast.
Therefore I have my suspicions that I might be doing something wrong.

Here are examples of the graphs that I got:


One of my models is:

m<-occu(~1~Area+Crops+Dense_wood+Peirmeter+Slope+VSI, data=ms)

For the graph of Dense_wood (plot at the right) the script I'm using is:

plotDat=data.frame(Dense_wood=seq(from=0, to=1, length=100), Area=mean(ms$Area), Crops=mean(ms$Crops), Perimeter=mean(ms$Peirmeter), Slope=mean(ms$Slope), VSI=mean(ms$VSI))

Pred<-predict(m, plotDat, type="state")

plot(plotDat$Dense_wood, Pred$Predicted, type="l", ylim=0:1)


Is there anything that looks wrong with this script?

Many thanks in advance for any reply.


Best,
Ana

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] plot occupancy probabilities: very steepy curves
parts:
Dear Ana-Maria,

I don't think you are doing anything wrong, but perhaps there is something wrong with the data ? Occupancy models are in essence a sort of logistic regression models. There is an issue in logistc regression called 'complete separation' (Gelman and Hill book has a section on this, surely also elsewhere). This is when there is strictly no overlap between covariates values for cases with a 0 response and those with a 1 response. In this case, the slope estimate is infinity (I think) and computations break down. Gelman shows that this can be mitigated with just a little bit of additional information provided in the prior of a Bayesian analysis of such a model. We have noted cases of probable complete separation in the application of a dynamic occupancy model (Kery et al., JBiog, 2013), where the predictions of occupancy from some complex models were essentially binary (i.e., either very close to 0 or very close to 1). We then simplified the model and the problem went away.

I don't know whether this is really the case in your example. How does the model fit summary look like for one of your models ? Does the problem appear also when you fit very simple models (e.g., with only a single covariate).

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: plot occupancy probabilities: very steepy curves
parts:
Dear Kery,

many thanks for your answer and for mentioning the 'complete separation' issu. I'm glad to hear that there's nothing wrong!
The output of the model I posted is:

Occupancy:
                          Estimate   SE         z          P(>|z|)
(Intercept)              -103     2646    -0.0390    0.969
Area                       -43      495       -0.0869    0.931
Crops                     181     1622      0.1113     0.911
Densewood           123      668        0.1849    0.853
Perimeter                67       927        0.0723    0.942
Slope                    187      1677       0.1116    0.911
VSI             -170  544 -0.3116   0.755

Detection:
 Estimate    SE    z P(>|z|)
      1.8 0.765 2.35  0.0189

Each selected model is the results of a selection process based on AIC, AUC, Kappa, PCC and RN² as model accuracy evaluators, after having generated all possible models with different variables combination. That's why model simplification might not be possible in this case. And, yes, actually when ploting the prediction of a model containing only the variable of interest, the curve increases gradually.
However, that's exactly what I found , and is, that the effect of each variable depends on the "context" (so, the values of the other variables) and i think that reporting graphs of the model with only one variab just doesn't what I really found.

But I think that now I have a hint on how to discuss this.
Many thanks!

Best regards,
Ana.

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: plot occupancy probabilities: very steepy curves
parts:
Your detection probability is estimated to be 0.86 for a single visit.  Even if you only have typically 2 visits per site, that results in a minimum of 0.98 (= 1- (1-0.86)^2) probability of at least one detection per site.  Therefore, you could likely get away with just performing logistic regression.  And packages that perform logistic regression will likely give you informative warnings or error messages if you have complete separation.

The huge standard errors compared to the estimates of all of the occupancy parameters is also an indication that something is not quite right.

Jim
